claude.sample_unit: adults in a community-based cohort (Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study)

links.outcome: Effect of local recalibration-in-the-large on predicted risk, sensitivity, and net benefit
links.effect: Recalibration raised mean predicted risk in men from 4.2% to 7.6%, sensitivity from 62.4% to 79.9% at 5% threshold; net benefit rose modestly (0.0356 to 0.040 in men); NRI +61% men, +79% women.
links.quote: Calibration-in-the-large improved model performance in both sexes, most notably in men, increasing mean predicted risks to 7.6% in men and 4.3% in women.

links.outcome: Calibration of PREVENT on a local cohort versus developer evidence
links.effect: Original model underestimated risk in men (mean predicted 4.2% vs observed ASCVD incidence higher) while well calibrated in women; AUC 0.84 women, 0.76 men.
links.quote: The basic model was well calibrated for women, particularly at low-to-intermediate risk levels, but underestimated risk in men.

links.outcome: Generalization of US-developed model to a new Iranian population
links.effect: PREVENT underestimated risk in Iranian men, needing recalibration; sensitivity 62.4% in men at 5% threshold before recalibration.
links.quote: However, the original model underestimated risk in Iranian men, indicating the need for recalibration to improve alignment with the local risk profile.

links.outcome: Dataset shift between US development and Iranian population affecting calibration
links.effect: Model developed in US underestimated risk in Iranian men; authors attribute differences to age distribution, baseline risk, follow-up, and population differences.
links.quote: Differences in discrimination across studies are likely attributable to variations in the age distribution, baseline risk, and follow-up duration of the study population.

links.effect: AUC 0.84 (0.82-0.86) in women vs 0.76 (0.74-0.78) in men; risk underestimated in men but not women.
links.quote: Using the published 10-year logistic PREVENT equations, discrimination was higher in women (AUC 0.84 [0.82–0.86]) than in men (AUC 0.76 [0.74–0.78]) (Fig. 1 ).

links.effect: In men, recalibration corrected underestimation, improving predicted risk from 4.2 to 7.6% and sensitivity from 62% to 80%.
links.quote: The model initially underestimated risk in men, which was corrected by recalibration, improving predicted risk from 4.2 to 7.6% and sensitivity from 62% to 80%.

links.effect: NRI was 79.0% (77.0–80.0) in women and 61.0% (59.0–63.0) in men versus original.
links.quote: The cut-point–based net reclassification improvement (NRI%, 95% CI) was 79.0% (77.0–80.0) in women and 61.0% (59.0–63.0) in men, indicating improved risk classification with calibration-in-the-large compared with the original model.

links.effect: AUC was 0.84 [0.82–0.86] in women and 0.76 [0.74–0.78] in men.
links.quote: Using the published 10-year logistic PREVENT equations, discrimination was higher in women (AUC 0.84 [0.82–0.86]) than in men (AUC 0.76 [0.74–0.78]) (Fig. 1 ).

links.effect: The basic model was well calibrated in women at low-to-intermediate risk levels, but underestimated 10-year ASCVD risk in men (mean predicted risk 4.2% vs 7.6% after recalibration).
links.quote: The basic model was well calibrated for women, particularly at low-to-intermediate risk levels, but underestimated risk in men.

links.outcome: ASCVD risk estimation and sensitivity after local recalibration
links.effect: Recalibration corrected initial risk underestimation in men, increasing predicted risk from 4.2% to 7.6% and sensitivity from 62% to 80%, while improving net reclassification by 61% in men and 79% in women.
links.quote: The model initially underestimated risk in men, which was corrected by recalibration, improving predicted risk from 4.2 to 7.6% and sensitivity from 62% to 80%.
